title: Completed Jacobian presentation of a finite algebra etale off an ideal
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian ring, $I\subseteq A$ an ideal, and suppose $A$ is $I$-adically complete [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Let $E$ be a commutative $A$-algebra finite as an $A$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] such that $\operatorname{Spec}E\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is etale over $\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus V(I)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-etale-morphism]. Then there exist an integer $r\geq0$, a surjective $A$-algebra homomorphism $P=A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]^\wedge\to E$ from the $I$-adic completion of the polynomial ring [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], its kernel $J$, and an integer $c\geq0$ such that $I^c$ annihilates both the kernel and the cokernel of the $E$-linear map $\delta:J/J^2\to E^{\oplus r}$, $f\bmod J^2\mapsto (\partial f/\partial x_i\bmod J)_{i=1}^r$. The partial derivatives on $P$ are obtained by continuity from polynomial differentiation. The ring $E$ is $I$-adically complete and $E/IE$ is a finite type $A/I$-algebra.

source.place: Tags 0AJP (lemma-topologically-finite-type), 0ALQ (lemma-rig-etale), part (1), and 0AJU (lemma-equivalent-with-artin), condition (3), applied to a finite algebra over a complete base; finiteness implies completeness over the complete Noetherian base by algebra.tex Tag 00MA (lemma-completion-tensor), part (3).

proof.text: The finite-module completeness theorem applied to the finite $A$-module $E$ makes the canonical map $E\to\widehat E$ bijective; it is a ring map, so is an $A$-algebra isomorphism. A finite list of module generators also generates $E$ as an $A$-algebra: every element is already a linear polynomial in them. Reducing those generators modulo $IE$ proves that $E/IE$ is a finite type $A/I$-algebra.

source.place: Finite-type observation in the proof of Tag 0ALQ; completeness is algebra.tex Tag 00MA (lemma-completion-tensor), part (3).

proof.text: By the finite-type Noetherian finite-presentation theorem, choose $r\geq0$ and a surjection $\alpha:S=A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]\twoheadrightarrow E$ whose kernel $K$ is finitely generated. The ordinary conormal criterion defines the well-defined $E$-linear differential $d_0:K/K^2\to E^{\oplus r}$ by polynomial partial derivatives. Put $U=\ker d_0$ and $V=\operatorname{coker}d_0$. The images of a finite list of ideal generators of $K$ generate $K/K^2$ over $E=S/K$, and the standard basis generates $V$. The ring $E$ is Noetherian because it is finite over $A$; hence the Noetherian submodule theorem makes $U$ finite as well.

source.place: Tag 0ALQ (lemma-rig-etale), ordinary finite-type presentation and finite cohomology; algebra.tex Tags 00FP, 00U1, 00FN, 00IK.

proof.text: Fix $a\in I$ and let $g$ be its image in $E$. The principal-open and basic-open pullback statements identify the inverse image of $D(a)$ with $\operatorname{Spec}E_g$, so the hypothesis says $\operatorname{Spec}E_g\to\operatorname{Spec}A_a$ is etale. The inclusion $\operatorname{Spec}A_a\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}A$ is an open immersion, so the etale composition lemma makes $\operatorname{Spec}E_g\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ etale. Use the principal-localization presentation $\beta:S[t]\twoheadrightarrow E_g$, $t\mapsto1/g$. Its kernel is generated by $K$ and $at-1$, hence is finitely generated. The ordinary conormal criterion says its conormal differential is bijective. By the Kähler basis lemma for polynomial rings, $\Omega_{S/A}\otimes_SE_g$ and $\Omega_{S[t]/A}\otimes_{S[t]}E_g$ are free on the $\mathrm dx_i$ (and $\mathrm dt$) with $\mathrm df\otimes1=\sum_i\partial f/\partial x_i\,\mathrm dx_i$ (plus $\partial f/\partial t\,\mathrm dt$), so the differentials of $\mathrm{NL}(\alpha)\otimes_EE_g$ and $\mathrm{NL}(\beta)$ are $(d_0)_g$ and the conormal-criterion differential of $\beta$. The principal-localization naive-cotangent lemma (with $f=a\in S$, $\alpha(a)=g$) decomposes the latter into $(d_0)_g$ and the invertible map $E_g\xrightarrow{g}E_g$. Its injectivity and cokernel clauses therefore show that $(d_0)_g$ is bijective.

source.place: Tag 0ALQ, converse paragraph; algebra.tex Tags 00U1 and 08JZ (lemma-principal-localization-NL); morphisms.tex open-immersion and composition properties of etale maps.

proof.text: Apply exactness of module localization to $0\to U\to K/K^2\xrightarrow{d_0}E^{\oplus r}\to V\to0$ at powers of $g$. Step 3 gives $U_g=V_g=0$. For each of these finite $E$-modules $M$, choose generators $m_1,\ldots,m_t$. The zero-fraction criterion says $m_j/1=0$ precisely when some $g^{n_j}m_j=0$. Taking the maximum of the finitely many exponents (zero if there are no generators) gives a power of $g$ killing $M$. Thus, for every $a\in I$, a single power of $a$ kills both $U$ and $V$.

source.place: Tag 0ALQ, converse paragraph: etaleness after inverting a gives power torsion; algebra.tex Tag 00CS and the fraction equivalence relation.

proof.text: Choose generators $a_1,\ldots,a_s$ of $I$, using that $A$ is Noetherian. For each $i$, Step 4 gives an integer $n_i\geq1$ such that $a_i^{n_i}$ kills both $U$ and $V$. If $s>0$, put $c=1+\sum_i(n_i-1)$. Every monomial of degree $c$ in the $a_i$ has some exponent at least $n_i$, and consequently annihilates both modules. Such monomials generate $I^c$, proving $I^cU=I^cV=0$. If $s=0$ then $I=0$, and $c=1$ works directly.

source.place: Tag 0ALQ, converse paragraph: combine the powers for finitely many generators of I; explicit monomial argument.

proof.text: Apply the polynomial-conormal completion comparison to $\alpha:S\twoheadrightarrow E$ and $I$. It gives a surjection $P=S^\wedge\twoheadrightarrow\widehat E$ with kernel $J=KP$, identifies $J/J^2$ with $(K/K^2)\otimes_E\widehat E$, and identifies its continuous-derivative differential with $d_0\otimes_E\widehat E$. Compose with the inverse of $E\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat E$ from Step 1. Explicitly $m\otimes\widehat e\mapsto e m$ identifies $(K/K^2)\otimes_E\widehat E$ with $K/K^2$, with inverse $m\mapsto m\otimes1$, and similarly for $E^{\oplus r}$. The comparison therefore identifies the completed differential $\delta$ with $d_0$ over $E$ itself. Its kernel and cokernel are $U$ and $V$, so Step 5 supplies the required $c$. Step 1 already proved the completeness and reduction assertions.
